SOURCE: "Delta Lake: High-Performance ACID Table Storage over Cloud Object Stores", Armbrust, Das, Sun, Yavuz, Zhu, ... Boncz, Ghodsi, ... Xin, Zaharia (Databricks, CWI, UC Berkeley, Stanford). PVLDB 13(12): 3411-3424, 2020 (peer-reviewed venue, VLDB 2020). DOI 10.14778/3415478.3415560.

COVERAGE: about 84,000 of 90,353 chars read, in full through the conclusion (pp. 1-12) and the start of the reference list. The remaining ~6k chars are references only, skimmed for origins. The text extracted cleanly. Figure 4 and 6 bar values come from axis text and are only partly legible. Page numbers below are PDF pages (journal pages 3411+, so PDF p.N = 3410+N).

VERIFICATION OF YOUR NOTE'S CITATIONS
1. VERIFIED, 1000 keys per call, tens to hundreds of ms (p.3, sec 2.1): "S3's LIST only returns up to 1000 keys per call, and each call takes tens to hundreds of milliseconds, so it can take minutes to list a dataset with millions of objects using a sequential implementation." Repeated in 2.3: "S3's LIST operations can only return up to 1000 objects per requests, and take tens to hundreds of milliseconds, so clients need to issue hundreds of LISTs in parallel".
2. VERIFIED, with a caveat. It is anecdotal and covers 2014-2016 (p.1, sec 1): "Anecdotally, in the first few years of Databricks' cloud service (2014–2016), around half the support escalations we received were due to data corruption, consistency or performance issues due to cloud storage strategies (e.g., undoing the effect of a crashed update job, or improving the performance of a query that reads tens of thousands of objects)." The note says "corruption/consistency/performance" and the paper adds "due to cloud storage strategies". Follow-up (p.2): "Anecdotally, Delta Lake reduced the fraction of support issues about cloud storage at Databricks from a half to nearly none."
3. VERIFIED (p.11, sec 6.1, Fig 4). Setup: "16-node AWS clusters of i3.2xlarge VMs (where each VM has 8 vCPUs, 61 GB RAM and 1.9 TB SSD storage) using Databricks and a popular cloud vendor that offers hosted Apache Hive and Presto. We then created small tables with 33,000,000 rows but between 1000 and 1,000,000 partitions in S3, to measure just the metadata overhead of a large number of partitions, and ran a simple query that sums all the records."
   - Quote: "Hive takes more than an hour to find the objects in a table with only 10,000 partitions ... and Presto takes more than an hour for 100,000 partitions. Databricks Runtime listing Parquet files completes in 450 seconds with 100,000 partitions, largely because we have optimized it to run LIST requests in parallel across the cluster. However, Delta Lake takes 108 seconds even with 1 million partitions, and only 17 seconds if the log is cached on SSDs."
   - Caveats for the note: the Hive and Presto systems are a "popular cloud vendor" hosted service, not named and not vanilla open source. Fig 4 caption: "The non-Delta systems took over an hour for 1 million partitions so we do not include their results there." Databricks Parquet listing took 450 s at 100,000 partitions (a useful extra comparator). The query is a simple sum, so it measures metadata overhead only. The "no cache" Delta run is the 108 s figure.
4. VERIFIED (p.5 sec 3.1.3 and p.6 sec 3.2.2 step 5). "By default, our clients write checkpoints every 10 transactions." Also: "(In practice, our implementations do this every 10 records by default.)" Checkpoint format: "Checkpoints store all the non-redundant actions in the table's log up to a certain log record ID, in Parquet format." Checkpointing only affects performance, not correctness: "a client failure anywhere during this step will not corrupt the data."

OTHER KEY CLAIMS (ranked)
- Core design: object membership of a table is kept in a write-ahead log (JSON files in _delta_log) stored in the object store itself, with data in Parquet. "no servers need to be running to maintain state for a Delta table". Writes use optimistic concurrency. (p.2)
  quote: "we maintain information about which objects are part of a Delta table in an ACID manner, using a write-ahead log that is itself stored in the cloud object store."
- Writes are serializable. Read-only transactions get snapshot isolation. "all transactions that perform writes are serializable, leading to a serial schedule in increasing order of log record IDs." (p.7, sec 3.3)
- Commit atomicity depends on the store (p.6, sec 3.2.2). GCS and Azure Blob use atomic put-if-absent. HDFS and ADLS use atomic rename. S3 lacks both, so Databricks uses a separate lightweight coordination service for log writes only. The open source Spark connector uses in-memory state per driver, so concurrency across clusters is not covered there. (A custom LogStore API is offered.)
- Write rate: "the latency of writes to object stores can be tens to hundreds of milliseconds, limiting the write transaction rate to several transactions per second", judged sufficient for virtually all current applications. (p.7, sec 3.4)
- Read protocol (p.6, sec 3.2.1): read _last_checkpoint, LIST from that ID, rebuild state from checkpoint plus later JSON, use min/max stats to prune, read data. It tolerates eventual consistency. A stale _last_checkpoint is fine. Zero-padded IDs make lexicographic LIST work.
- Z-order (p.11, sec 6.2): a synthetic 100-object table of random IPs/ports. Quote: "Z-ordering by all four columns allows skipping at least 43% of the Parquet objects for queries in each dimension, and 54% on average ... (compared to 25% for the single sort order)." Fig 5 shows a global sort skipping 99% on sourceIP and 0% on the other fields. A 500 TB network dataset "were able to skip 93% of the data".
- TPC-DS (p.11, sec 6.3, Fig 6): 1 TB in S3, 1 master plus 8 i3.2xlarge workers, average of 3 runs. Axis values 0.93, 0.99, 1.44 and 3.76 h appear in the extraction. Assuming the order follows the legend, they map to Databricks Delta, Databricks Parquet, 3rd-party Spark and 3rd-party Presto. Check that mapping against the figure. Text says Delta beats all, mainly by speeding the longer queries, and "some of Delta Lake's advantages handling large numbers of partitions do not manifest because many tables are small".
- Write overhead (p.11-12, sec 6.4, Fig 7): loading 400 GB of TPC-DS store_sales from CSV, 1 master plus 8 workers. Delta write is similar to Parquet, so stats collection adds no significant overhead. No numbers are given in the text.
- Scale and adoption: "thousands of Databricks customers that process exabytes of data per day", around half of the Databricks workload. Speedups "as high as 100×" in extreme cases (the security and bioinformatics cases).
- OPTIMIZE default target object size is 1 GB. Checkpoint contents, tombstones and dataChange flag details are on pp.5, 7.
- S3 object store facts (p.3, sec 2.3): per-read base latency 5-10 ms, roughly 50-100 MB/s per read, and 8-10 parallel reads to saturate 10 Gbps. S3 LIST is always eventually consistent (as of 2020). This has dated, since S3 later became strongly consistent.
- Streaming (p.8, sec 4.3): "latency on the order of seconds" is feasible, using the txn (appId, version) action for exactly-once writes.
- Caching (p.8, sec 4.5): the SSD cache is safe because data, log and checkpoint objects are immutable. i3 instances cost "roughly 50% higher" than m5.
- Related work (p.12, sec 8): Hudi and Iceberg are the closest systems. The paper says Hudi supports only one writer at a time, and that Hive ACID bottlenecks on its metastore with millions of partitions.

LIMITS
- Authors concede (sec 7, p.12): transactions are serializable within a single table only. Streaming latency is bounded by object store latency, so millisecond latency is hard. There are no secondary indexes beyond per-file min/max stats (a Bloom filter prototype is mentioned). Commit rate is limited to several per second.
- The 50% support-escalation figure is explicitly "anecdotally", not measured.
- Benchmarks are run by Databricks on its own runtime against an unnamed third-party Hive/Presto service. The authors say the Spark gap comes from Databricks Runtime optimizations (both Spark 2.4). Not independent. The table is small (33M rows) by design, to isolate metadata cost.
- Z-order experiment is synthetic uniform-random data. Several features (Z-order, AUTO OPTIMIZE, SSD cache) are Databricks-service features, not in open source Delta at the time (the paper says the "cache" is in the Databricks service).
- Dated: S3 eventual-consistent LIST and no put-if-absent were true in 2020. Later changes in S3 consistency are not in the paper. Hudi and Iceberg comparisons reflect 2020.

BUILDS ON: Parquet and ORC columnar formats; Hive partition directory layout (Apache Hive, Thusoo 2009 [45] as printed in the ref list); MVCC for time travel; Z-order curve (Morton, ref [35]); Snowflake's metadata-service design (Dageville et al., ref [23]) as the contrasting "closed-world" approach; Hive ACID [32]; Spark SQL and Structured Streaming (Armbrust et al. 2015, 2018 [14, 16]); C-Store (Stonebraker, ref [43]); Brantner et al. OLTP on S3 [20]; bolt-on consistency [19]; Aurora [49]; Hudi and Iceberg as concurrent work. I did not verify the reference-list entries beyond the first ~16, so check the author and year printed in the PDF before citing.

CODE: Time-travel repair example (p.7, sec 4.1), verbatim:
MERGE INTO mytable target
USING mytable TIMESTAMP AS OF <old_date> source
ON source.userId = target.userId
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
Also the log layout in Fig 2 (p.4): mytable/date=2020-01-01/...parquet, _delta_log/000001.json ... 000003.json, 000003.parquet, 000004.json, 000005.json, _last_checkpoint (contains {version: "000003"}).

FIGURES:
- Fig 2 (p.4): objects stored in a sample Delta table. It shows the data objects, JSON log records, a checkpoint at 000003.parquet and _last_checkpoint. It is the fastest way to explain the log layout.
- Fig 4 (p.11): query time versus partition count (1000 to 1M, log scale), for Delta with cache, Delta without cache, Databricks Parquet, 3rd-party Presto and 3rd-party Hive. It is the source of the 108 s and 17 s numbers.
- Fig 5 (p.11): percent of objects skipped, global sort versus Z-order, per filter field.
- Fig 1 (p.2): pipeline with a message queue, object store and warehouses versus Delta only.
- Fig 6 (p.11): TPC-DS power test duration. Fig 7 (p.12): 400 GB load time.
I did not run the captions script, so these captions come from the extraction.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Some ligature characters (ﬁ, ﬂ) appear in the extraction. I normalised nothing inside the quotes beyond that, so the quotes keep the ligatures, and a string search for "file" in the raw text will miss them. Figure bar values are not extracted, only axis labels, so exact TPC-DS durations per system need a check against the figure itself.
